arXiv:2610.37585v1 [cs.AI] 27 Oct 2026

Timestral

Abstract

We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face11 1 https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/timestral and inference code on GitHub22 2 https://github.com/mistralai/timestral.

Webpage: https://mistral.ai/news/timestral

1 Introduction

\Acp

tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024). Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates (Khwaja et al., 2026; Ansari et al., 2025; Podest et al., 2026; Meyer et al., 2026). These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use.

Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0 (Ansari et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026) sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two. Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass. To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively. cpm (cpm), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3 (Auer et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026; Jain and Sen, 2026), achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence. The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking. Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden.

We introduce Timestral, a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost. Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through dhf (dhf), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality. The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context. Timestral-209M sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. As shown in Figure 1, all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics. Timestral-123M already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters.

This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them:

  • •

    dhf. We introduce dhf, a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens. dhf preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking.

  • •

    Covariate conditioning within dhf. We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention. This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values.

  • •

    A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost. We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters. The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval (Aksu et al., 2024), TIME (Qiao et al., 2026), and fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026).

2 Background

We first describe tsfm within the framework of pfn, which interprets forecasting as amortised posterior inference (Section 2.1). We then review how current tsfm model dependencies across variates and over time, and the drawbacks that motivate the design of Timestral (Section 2.2).

2.1 Time Series Foundation Models as Prior-Data Fitted Networks

Synthetic data has become a standard ingredient of tsfm training, and its share has generally grown. TimesFM mixes 20% synthetic series built from ARMA processes, seasonal patterns, trends, and steps (Das et al., 2024); Chronos samples 10% of its training series from KernelSynth, a Gaussian-process generator (Ansari et al., 2024); and TiRex draws about a third of its training series from an extended KernelSynth generator (Auer et al., 2025). More recent models rely on synthetic data more heavily: 57.5% of Toto-2.0’s pretraining mix is generated with TempoPFN’s generators (Khwaja et al., 2026), and Chronos-2 learns its multivariate and covariate capabilities from synthetic data only, with a variant trained without any real data performing only slightly worse than the full model (Ansari et al., 2025).

At the other end, time series pfn such as ForecastPFN, Mamba4Cast, TimePFN, and TempoPFN are trained exclusively on synthetic data (Dooley et al., 2023; Bhethanabhotla et al., 2024; Taga et al., 2025; Moroshan et al., 2026).

Timestral follows this direction: it is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data, and a significant part of our effort went into designing the generating processes. The pfn framework provides a principled view of this choice, in which the generators define a prior over processes and forecasting becomes approximate Bayesian inference under that prior.

Given the observed history 𝐲1:t\mathbf{y}_{1:t} of the target variates (the context), the task is to produce forecasts 𝐲^t+1:t+H\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t+1:t+H} for the next HH time steps. From a Bayesian perspective, a probabilistic forecast should follow the ppd (ppd). If the series is generated by an unknown process ff drawn from a prior p⁡(f)p(f), the ppd integrates over all processes consistent with the context,

p(𝐲t+1:t+H∣𝐲1:t)=∫p(𝐲t+1:t+H∣𝐲1:t,f)p(f∣𝐲1:t)df.p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H}\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t})=\int p(\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H}\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t},f)\,p(f\mid\mathbf{y}_{1:t})\,\mathrm{d}f. (1)

It accounts for both the noise of a given process and the uncertainty about which process generated the context. Covariates enter as further conditioning variables and are omitted for brevity.

\Acp

pfn (Müller et al., 2022) learn to approximate the ppd during training: each training example draws a process f∼p⁡(f)f\sim p(f) and a dataset from ff, and the network predicts held-out values from the observed ones. In tabular pfn (Hollmann et al., 2023; Hollmann et al., 2025), ff can be a random scm that generates context rows of features and targets; the network then predicts the targets of further rows from their features. In time series pfn, ff generates a context 𝐲1:t\mathbf{y}_{1:t} (optionally with covariates) and the network predicts its continuation 𝐲t+1:t+H\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H} as in Equation 1. When trained with the negative log-likelihood, the network’s optimal prediction is the ppd. The network thus amortises posterior inference over ff: instead of fitting a model to each new series, it infers from the context which processes are plausible and approximates the ppd in a single forward pass.

\Acp

tsfm differ from this setting in two respects but admit the same interpretation. First, many recent tsfm are trained with the pinball loss (Auer et al., 2025; Ansari et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026). With the pinball loss, the optimal prediction is not the full ppd but its quantiles (Koenker and Bassett, 1978): for each future time step and quantile level τ\tau, the network learns the τ\tau-quantile of the ppd at that time step. Second, their prior is not defined by synthetic generators alone: real series, viewed as draws from unknown processes, are also used, for example in continued training as in recent tabular pfn (Garg et al., 2025), so the full training data and its augmentations form the prior.

In this view, a tsfm approximates the ppd under the prior defined by its training data. This prior determines which processes are plausible for a given context and thus how uncertain the forecasts are. A prior with too much unpredictable variability widens forecasts even for regular series, whereas one with too little makes the model overconfident. The composition of the training data is therefore a central design choice for tsfm.

2.2 Time Series Foundation Model Architectures

Patch-based forecasting.

Following PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023), most modern tsfm represent a time series as a sequence of non-overlapping patches (Das et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024; Ansari et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026; Jain and Sen, 2026). Each patch ii of PP consecutive time steps of a target variate is mapped to a token embedding 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}, reducing the token sequence length by a factor of PP. A sequence-modelling backbone, such as a Transformer, state-space model, or rnn, processes these context tokens and computes patch-based representations 𝐡j\mathbf{h}_{j} for the forecast horizon. A prediction head maps these representations back to time-step resolution, producing forecasts for future patch jj. This is commonly a quantile head, which predicts conditional quantiles for each time step to represent forecast uncertainty (Ansari et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026).

Multivariate forecasting and covariates.

Multivariate forecasting allows predictions for each target variate to depend on both its own history and the histories of other target variates. Covariates 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} provide additional inputs without themselves being forecast. Past-only covariates (patch embeddings 𝐜ipast\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{past}}_{i}) supply historical values, while known-future covariates (patch embeddings 𝐜ifut\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{fut}}_{i}) supply both historical values and values known in advance over the forecast horizon. Toto-2.0 and Chronos-2 use cross-variate attention to exchange information between variates at the same patch position. Toto-2.0 replaces temporal attention in its final Transformer block with variate attention, whereas Chronos-2 applies both temporal and variate attention in every Transformer block (Khwaja et al., 2026; Ansari et al., 2025). Chronos-2 supports both covariate types within its group-attention formulation.

Bidirectional temporal modelling.

Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 (Ansari et al., 2025) and Falcon-2.0 (Xia et al., 2026) process the observed context together with tokens at future prediction positions, without exposing future values of the target variates. Figure 2(a) illustrates this construction with context embeddings 𝐯0,…,𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{3} and prediction tokens 𝐩4,…,𝐩6\mathbf{p}_{4},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{6}. Bidirectional attention lets all positions exchange information; the prediction head maps the final representations at future positions to forecasts. Training on forecasts starting at different points in a series generally requires encoding each context separately, because bidirectional attention lets later observations influence earlier context representations.

Causal temporal modelling.

Causal temporal modelling restricts each context representation to values of target variates and past-only covariates at the current and preceding patch positions. Known-future covariate values may additionally be used beyond this cutoff. Causal decoder-only models such as TimesFM (Das et al., 2024), Toto (Cohen et al., 2025), and Timer (Liu et al., 2024) map the representation at each position to a forecast of the following patch (Figure 2(b)). Trained on fully observed sequences, a single forward pass thus provides a one-patch-ahead forecast from every position of the sequence, reusing the shared history instead of re-encoding it for each forecast. Patch-wise ar (ar) inference extends the horizon by feeding decoded predictions back as inputs before predicting the next patch. ar forecasting can estimate uncertainty over longer horizons by sampling multiple trajectories (Salinas et al., 2020). However, sampling multiple trajectories adds significant computational cost, and feeding predictions back into the model can compound errors (Bengio et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2018).

cpm.

cpm trains models to forecast several future patches without feeding intermediate predictions back as inputs. First introduced in TiRex (Auer et al., 2025) and later adapted to Transformers in Toto-2.0 (Khwaja et al., 2026), cpm masks consecutive input patches during training, teaching the model to forecast several patches ahead from the preceding context. A masked patch has all its values hidden from the model but remains in the input sequence as a token with embedding 𝐦i\mathbf{m}_{i}. A run of rr masked patches following a visible patch therefore allows forecasts up to r+1r+1 patches ahead (Figure 3(a)).

At inference, the input sequence is constructed from the observed context followed by a block of masked patches covering the forecast horizon (Figure 3(b)). The model then forecasts the whole block in one forward pass, without feeding intermediate predictions back as inputs. During training, however, patches masked to create longer-horizon forecasts also remain unavailable as observations for forecasts starting later in the sequence. The masking pattern therefore determines both the forecast horizons encountered during training and the observations available as context. In contrast, dhf, introduced in Section 3.1, separates horizon sampling from context masking while retaining shared causal context computation.

3 Timestral

Timestral is a causal encoder-only model for multivariate forecasting that supports both past-only and known-future covariates (Figure 4). As in bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0, forecasts are produced at dedicated prediction tokens rather than from context representations; unlike them, the context is encoded causally. Two modelling choices define the dependency structure of Timestral, along time and across variates. Along time, dhf (Section 3.1) decouples the context from the forecast horizon: prediction tokens attend to the context without affecting it. Across variates (Section 3.2), targets exchange information with each other and receive information from covariates, but never pass information to them; only known-future covariates contribute values from later patches, including the forecast horizon. Section 3.3 describes the patch embedding, normalisation, Transformer backbone, and quantile head.

3.1 Temporal Modelling via dhf

dhf uses separate tokens for observed context patches and for forecast positions. For simplicity, we describe dhf for a single target variate. Temporal attention operates on each variate separately, and all variates of a series share the same forecast blocks. The context consists of one token 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} per patch ii, processed with causal attention, so the representation of patch ii depends only on patches 0,…,i0,\ldots,i. As shown in Figure 5, a forecast block covering patches b,…,b+k−1b,\ldots,b+k-1 adds prediction tokens 𝐩b,…,𝐩b+k−1\mathbf{p}_{b},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{b+k-1}. These are copies of a single learned embedding, distinguished by their temporal position: 𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{j} takes the same temporal position as the context token 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j}. Both kinds of tokens are processed by the same Transformer, with shared parameters. Each 𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{j} attends to the context tokens before its block and to the prediction tokens 𝐩b,…,𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{b},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{j} of its own block, whereas context tokens never attend to prediction tokens. Context and prediction tokens thus form two separate streams. The resulting output 𝐡j\mathbf{h}_{j} is passed to the prediction head to forecast patch jj and therefore depends only on 𝐯0,…,𝐯b−1\mathbf{v}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{b-1} and 𝐩b,…,𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{b},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{j}. Outputs at context tokens are not passed to the prediction head and receive no direct loss.

To train forecasts at many forecast distances, each training sequence is tiled into consecutive forecast blocks whose lengths are sampled from a block-length distribution. A block of length kk contains one forecast at each distance 1,…,k1,\ldots,k, so this distribution determines how often each forecast distance is trained. Because context tokens never attend to prediction tokens, the context representations are computed once and shared by all blocks of a training sequence. As in causal decoder-only models (Figure 2(b)), a single training sequence thus provides training signal from forecasts at many starting points, but in dhf, the forecast from each starting point can extend several patches ahead.

Unlike cpm, dhf does not mask context patches to create longer forecast distances. In cpm, a forecast at distance dd requires masking the d−1d-1 patches before its target, and these patches are then also missing from the context of all later forecasts, so training longer forecast distances removes context. In dhf, each patch in a forecast block has two tokens during training: its prediction token, at which it is forecast, and its context token, which keeps its observed values available to later blocks. In Figure 5, for instance, the forecasts of the third block depend on 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2}, which cpm masks.

This decoupling has the following advantages. First, how often each forecast distance is trained can be tuned without side effects on the context. Second, missing data can be simulated independently of the forecast distances: optional missing-data augmentation hides variable-length gaps at arbitrary time steps rather than whole patches, which is closer to realistic missing-data distributions, and the hidden values are still scored as targets. Third, missing values, whether in the data or introduced by augmentation, are flagged in their context tokens and thus represented differently from forecast positions, whereas cpm represents a patch masked for forecasting in the same way as a fully missing patch. These advantages come at the cost of roughly doubling the number of tokens during training, since forecast blocks tile the full sequence so that every patch except the first serves as a forecast target.

At inference, a single forecast block follows the context, so forecasts up to the maximum block length of 32 patches (1,024 time steps) are produced in a single forward pass. Longer horizons can be forecast block by block, conditioning each block on the predicted medians of the previous ones, as in Toto-2.0 (Khwaja et al., 2026).

3.2 Multivariate and Covariate Modelling

Each variate of a multivariate series is represented by its own sequence of tokens and has one of three roles: target variate, past-only covariate, or known-future covariate (Figure 4). Every variate has context and prediction tokens, but only the outputs at prediction tokens of target variates are used as forecasts. Roles are not embedded in the tokens and enter the model only through the attention masks and the choice of normalisation (Section 3.3). Along time, target variates and past-only covariates are processed causally, as described in Section 3.1. The context tokens of known-future covariates instead attend over the entire window, including the forecast horizon, where they hold the known future values. Normalisation follows the same distinction (Section 3.3).

Similar to Chronos-2 and Toto-2.0 (Ansari et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026), variate attention exchanges information between the variates of a series at the same patch position, among context tokens and among prediction tokens. It uses no positional encoding, so the order of the variates does not affect the forecasts. To prevent future information leakage, known-future covariates attend only to each other. Otherwise, a known-future covariate could read the value of a target variate or past-only covariate at patch ii and, through its temporal attention, carry it back to earlier patches, from which it would reach the forecast of patch ii. Past-only covariates do not attend to target variates either; this is a modelling choice that treats covariates as exogenous, so that their representations do not depend on target values. Forecasts can thus use future values of known-future covariates, but never future values of target variates or past-only covariates.

During training, some variates in a random subset of multivariate series are assigned the role of past-only or known-future covariates, while the others remain target variates. These covariates are inputs only and are not scored, so ordinary multivariate series become forecasting tasks with covariates.

3.3 Architecture

Each patch of P=32P=32 time steps of a variate is embedded into a single token by a two-layer residual mlp (mlp). Its input consists of the PP normalised values and PP binary indicators of missing time steps, at which the values are set to zero, so that missing values are distinguished from observed zeros. Similar to previous work, values are standardised causally with the mean and standard deviation of all observed values of their variate up to the end of the current patch (Cohen et al., 2025), and an inverse hyperbolic sine is applied to the standardised values (Ansari et al., 2025). Known-future covariates, whose values are known over the entire window, are instead normalised with statistics over this window, and binary ones, such as holiday flags, are left unchanged.

The backbone is a pre-norm Transformer with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) and SwiGLU feed-forward layers (Shazeer, 2020). Each block applies temporal attention and a feed-forward layer, and every fourth block additionally applies variate attention between the two. Both attention types use gated attention with an elementwise sigmoid output gate (Qiu et al., 2025). Temporal attention encodes token positions with rotary position embeddings (Su et al., 2024) on half of each head’s dimensions. No timestamps, frequency information, or role or position embeddings are added; positions enter only through the rotary embeddings of temporal attention. Neither dropout nor stochastic depth is used.

After a final RMSNorm, a two-layer residual mlp maps each output 𝐡j\mathbf{h}_{j} to 21 quantiles for each of the PP time steps of patch jj. The head predicts the median directly and the other quantiles by adding or subtracting cumulative sums of positive (softplus) increments, preventing quantile crossing by construction. Each forecast patch is standardised with the statistics of all values up to the end of the preceding patch, and its predicted quantiles are mapped back to the original scale by inverting the asinh and this standardisation. Within a forecast block, these values include the earlier patches of the block, which are unknown at inference and are therefore replaced by their predicted medians. The same statistics are used during training to standardise the targets, so that training and inference match. Table 1 lists the model sizes.

4 Results

We describe the data and training setup shared by the four Timestral models, then report their forecasting performance on public benchmarks.

4.1 Training Setup

All four Timestral models are pretrained exclusively on synthetic data with a context length of 8,192 time steps and then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with a context length of 32,768 time steps for substantially fewer steps.

Training data.

The synthetic corpus includes both univariate signals and multivariate examples, covering temporal dynamics and cross-series dependencies. We generate univariate series with diverse trends, seasonal patterns, and noise characteristics across temporal resolutions. Additional patterns include regime changes, localised events, level shifts, and count-valued observations. We construct multivariate examples by introducing linear and nonlinear dependencies between base univariate signals, using structured synthetic priors (Ansari et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Naour et al., 2026; Podest et al., 2026). Selected variates serve as past-only or known-future covariates, providing training examples with different input availability patterns.

Training objective.

We train with the pinball loss (Koenker and Bassett, 1978), without auxiliary objectives. For a target value yy and a predicted quantile q^τ\hat{q}_{\tau} at level τ\tau, the loss is

ρτ​(e)=max⁡(τ​e,(τ−1)​e),e=y−q^τ.\rho_{\tau}(e)=\max\!\left(\tau e,\,(\tau-1)e\right),\qquad e=y-\hat{q}_{\tau}. (2)

Minimising this loss trains q^τ\hat{q}_{\tau} to estimate the conditional τ\tau-quantile of yy (Koenker and Bassett, 1978). The prediction head outputs 21 quantile levels, 𝒯={0.01,0.05,0.10,…,0.95,0.99}\mathcal{T}=\{0.01,0.05,0.10,\dots,0.95,0.99\}. We average the loss equally across quantile levels and scored positions:

ℒ=1|𝒯|​∑iwi​∑iwi​∑τ∈𝒯ρτ​(yi−q^τ,i),\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|\sum_{i}w_{i}}\sum_{i}w_{i}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\rho_{\tau}\!\left(y_{i}-\hat{q}_{\tau,i}\right), (3)

where ii indexes target values within forecast blocks and wiw_{i} is one for scored positions and zero otherwise. Only observed target values within a forecast horizon are scored. Context representations and covariates receive no direct loss; they are trained through their influence on the scored predictions. Targets and predictions are compared in the model’s normalised space, reducing differences in loss scale between series.

4.2 Forecasting Performance

We evaluate Timestral on GIFT-Eval (Aksu et al., 2024), TIME (Qiao et al., 2026), and fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026). On fev-bench, we report skill scores for mase (mase) and sql (sql). On GIFT-Eval, Timestral uses past-only covariates on the few datasets that provide them. On fev-bench, it uses the available past-only and known-future covariates according to each task’s input specification.

Timestral sets a new state of the art across GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench.

Figures 6, 7 and 8 compare all four Timestral sizes with other leading entries on each benchmark, and Table 3 in Appendix A reports the scores of all compared models. Timestral-209M ranks first on all six metrics among the models compared: it has the lowest mase and crps (crps) on GIFT-Eval and TIME and the highest mase and sql skill scores on fev-bench, using a single checkpoint. Pairwise win rates in Section A.3 complement these aggregate scores by measuring how often Timestral improves over each competitor. Section A.2 additionally reports results on the industrial benchmark IND-Eval (Haugland et al., 2026), where Timestral-209M, Timestral-123M, and Timestral-28M take the top three places.

Every Timestral size lies on the Pareto front.

Figure 1 plots accuracy against parameter count: all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front, and the smaller ones outperform much larger models. Timestral-123M ranks second on all six metrics, ahead of every model outside the family, and both Timestral-123M and Timestral-209M have fewer parameters than t0-gamma (256M) (The Forecasting Company, 2026) and TimesFM-3 (331M). Timestral-28M outperforms Chronos-2 and Toto-2.0-2.5B, about 4 and 90 times larger, on all six metrics, and on fev-bench Timestral-5M outperforms every Toto-2.0 model, including Toto-2.0-2.5B with about 480 times as many parameters.

4.3 Inference Speed

Timestral does not require a GPU at inference. A forecast of up to 1,024 time steps is produced in a single forward pass (Section 3.1), so its cost depends mainly on the context length and the number of variates. Table 2 reports the latency and throughput of each model for a representative workload: forecasting one day ahead (96 steps) of a univariate series without covariates, from about three weeks of 15-minute history (2,048 steps).

Setup.

We time the forecast method of the released inference package with the released checkpoints, end to end, with bfloat16 weights and torch.compile; the bfloat16 forecasts differ from float32 ones by less than 0.2%. Each forecast uses symmetric averaging: the model also forecasts the negated series and averages the reflected forecast with the original one, which requires two forward passes. CPU numbers are measured on a 48-core server CPU (AMD EPYC 9454) and GPU numbers on one NVIDIA H100, with PyTorch 2.14; we report the median over repeated runs after warm-up.

A forecast takes 17 to 113 ms on 8 CPU threads.

Latency grows with model size, and additional threads mainly benefit the larger models: from 1 to 8 threads, Timestral-209M becomes 3.1 times faster, whereas Timestral-5M is already as fast on a single core.

Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed.

Timestral-28M is 3.6 times faster than Timestral-209M, and Timestral-123M has about 0.2% higher GIFT-Eval mase than Timestral-209M at 75% of its latency (Figures 1 and 2).

Throughput.

One CPU core forecasts 3.5 (Timestral-209M) to 106 (Timestral-5M) series per second, so forecasting 100,000 series every 15 minutes requires 2 to 32 cores. One NVIDIA H100 forecasts 3,650 to 18,770 series per second, that is, 100,000 series in 5 to 27 seconds.

Context length and number of variates.

Figure 9 varies the context length and the number of variates. Up to 2,048 steps, latency changes little: it roughly doubles from 128 to 2,048 steps. Beyond, it grows nearly in proportion to the context, by about 9 to 12 times from 2,048 to 32,768 steps, the longest context used in training; at that length, a forecast takes 119 ms with Timestral-5M and 1.3 s with Timestral-209M. A series with 32 variates takes 7 to 15 times as long as a univariate series. Covariates cost more than target variates: one target with seven known-future covariates takes 1.7 to 2.0 times as long as eight target variates.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Timestral, a family of four foundation models with 5M to 209M parameters for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting. dhf separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that observed values serve both as forecast targets and as context for later forecasts, and longer forecast distances are trained without masking context. Role-aware attention masks let prediction tokens use known-future covariates at every forecast origin, while forecasts never use future values of target variates or past-only covariates. The models are pretrained exclusively on synthetic data and then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context.

Timestral-209M ranks first among the models compared on every reported metric of GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench using a single checkpoint. It leads by a wider margin on IND-Eval. Timestral-123M ranks second, ahead of every model outside the Timestral family, and all four sizes lie on the Pareto front of accuracy against size. Accuracy still improves from 123M to 209M parameters, which motivates training larger models. Beyond standalone forecasting, Timestral can be embedded in existing monitoring pipelines or combined with language models in agentic workflows. A further direction is to use the context representations as embeddings for tasks such as classification and anomaly detection.

Appendix A Detailed Results

This appendix expands on the results in Section 4. We report aggregate scores for all compared models on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, followed by an evaluation on IND-Eval, which focuses on industrial forecasting tasks. Pairwise win rates complement these aggregate results by showing how often each Timestral model outperforms the selected competitors.

A.1 GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench

Table 3 reports aggregate scores for all models included in the benchmark bars or Pareto plot at the date of the release (October 15th 2026). The table includes all four released Timestral sizes. Timestral-209M ranks first on all six metrics, and Timestral-123M ranks second, ahead of every model outside the Timestral family in this comparison.

A.2 IND-Eval

Benchmark.

We additionally evaluate Timestral on IND-Eval (Haugland et al., 2026), a public benchmark for forecasting in complex physical systems. It comprises 187 tasks covering applications in energy, manufacturing, and transport. Compared with general-purpose forecasting benchmarks, it emphasises finer sampling resolutions and multivariate targets.

Evaluation.

All IND-Eval results reported here come from our own evaluation runs, using publicly released checkpoints and inference code from the model authors’ public repositories under the official benchmark protocol. We re-evaluate TimesFM-3, Chronos-2, and TiRex-2, the three models studied by Haugland et al. (2026), and extend the comparison to t0-gamma, t0-beta, all five released Toto-2.0 sizes (4M, 22M, 313M, 1B, and 2.5B), and Granite-PatchTST-FM-r2, alongside all four Timestral sizes. All models are evaluated zero-shot, without fine-tuning, using the official IND-Eval context–target windows and a context capped at 4,096 time steps. We report nmase (nmase) and ncrps (ncrps) relative to Seasonal Naive. Each task score divides the model’s error by the corresponding error of Seasonal Naive; values below one indicate lower error. We first take the geometric mean of task scores within each dataset, then the geometric mean of the resulting dataset scores. This gives each dataset equal weight in the aggregate.

Aggregate results.

Figure 10 compares aggregate errors for all four Timestral sizes and the eleven competitors evaluated here. Timestral-209M ranks first among the models compared, with aggregate nmase of 0.646 and ncrps of 0.435. Relative to t0-gamma, the strongest model outside the Timestral family on both metrics (0.697 and 0.469), this is about 7% lower error. Accuracy improves at every increase in Timestral model size. Timestral-123M obtains 0.663 nmase and 0.441 ncrps, and Timestral-28M obtains 0.692 and 0.464, respectively; both remain ahead of every model outside the family on the two aggregates.

A.3 Pairwise Win Rates

Aggregate errors summarise overall forecasting accuracy, while pairwise win rates measure how often one model outperforms another across tasks. Figures 11, 12, 13 and 14 compare all four released Timestral sizes with the selected competitors on each benchmark. Each cell reports the row model’s win rate against the column model across the benchmark’s tasks, with lower error counting as a win and exact ties as half a win, following the fev definition (Shchur et al., 2026). Errors are compared before rounding, and all tasks receive equal weight.

We follow the official evaluation protocols for each benchmark; IND-Eval task errors come from our own evaluation runs described in Section A.2. For fev-bench, win rates use task errors rather than aggregate skill scores. Timestral-209M wins on a majority of tasks against every selected competitor on both metrics of each benchmark. Timestral-123M shows the same pattern on all four benchmarks.
